newsitem.title: CHILE: Chilean rebel suspect gives up after French asylum bid.
newsitem.headline: Chilean rebel suspect gives up after French asylum bid.

text.p: A Chilean leftist guerrilla suspect surrendered to police on Friday after holing himself up in the French embassy and demanding asylum to avoid arrest on weapons charges, Chilean officials said.
The accused member of the Manuel Rodriguez Patriotic Front, Domiciano Alberto Soto, and his sister walked into the embassy and requested asylum, alleging they were victims of political persecution.
They left about eight hours later, after French ambassador Gerard Cros told them their asylum request had been denied, police said.

Police arrested Soto as soon as he walked out of the building in Santiago's posh Providencia neighbourhood, while his sister, Maria Antonia Soto, was allowed to go free because she had no charges pending against her, police said.
"They walked out, and he was arrested immediately," said a police spokesman. "I guess they didn't get their asylum."

A military judge issued an arrest warrant for Soto on Monday on charges of smuggling weapons and issued another order the next day barring him from leaving the country, said deputy Interior Minister Belisario Velasco.

Police mounted a heavy presence around the embassy during the whole episode. French officials, eager to keep news of the asylum bid under wraps, for hours flatly denied there was any fleeing guerrilla inside until Velasco confirmed the rumours.
Police said Soto was charged with arms smuggling and indirect involvement in various guerrilla strikes, including the assassination of rightist Senator Jaime Guzman in 1991.

The Manuel Rodriguez group, named for a 19th century rebel against Spanish colonial rule, scored its most famous blow in 1986 when it wounded military ruler General Augusto Pinochet in an assassination attempt, in which five of Pinochet's bodyguards died.

The group, thought dormant since the early 1990s, leaped back to life in December when it rescued four of its leaders from jail in a daring helicopter raid which shocked Chilean public opinion and forced the head of the prison guards service to resign in disgrace.
Police later said they had strong indications of help in the rescue from the Irish Republican Army and sent investigators to Ireland and Britain to check out leads.
